A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same GIQ benchmark, and all supplied pages are readable. However, v1 ends at references on page 15 and v3 on page 14; neither includes the supplementary material or appendix repeatedly referenced in its text. This limits comparison of detailed results, ablations, and implementation information deferred there.

before.justification: V1 reports original reconstruction examples, symmetry-detection accuracies, mental-rotation experiments, and zero-shot classification results in Section 4.

after.justification: V3 reports original results for the same four tasks, expanded model comparisons, and a new 42-participant mental-rotation study.

M1.justification: Section 4.3 changes the principal MRT readout from linear probing of absolute embedding differences to a nonlinear probe. Section 4.2 also introduces nonlinear symmetry probes. These revise the probing component; the absolute-difference representation and stated symmetry loss remain unchanged.

E1.justification: The 224-polyhedron collection and four principal tasks remain. V3 substantially broadens evaluation scenarios through three-view classification inputs, classification from ground-truth point clouds, and a human MRT population of 42 participants. These introduce input conditions and a population absent from the reported v1 evaluations.

E2.justification: V3 Figure 3 adds VGGT, DUSt3R, and MASt3R to symmetry and MRT comparisons, plus a human MRT baseline. Figure 4 adds LLaVA-3D, ShapeLLM, and PointLLM to the four retained frontier classifiers. The reconstruction comparator set remains Shap-E, Stable Fast 3D, and OpenLRM.

E3.justification: Symmetry evaluation changes from a held-out set of 26 shapes to five-fold shape-disjoint cross-validation. For hard MRT, v1 describes mixed-pair training and testing, whereas v3 describes synthetic-only training followed by synthetic and synthetic-wild testing. V3 also introduces a timed human protocol: five easy and twenty hard questions, with 30 seconds per question.

E4.justification: V3 newly reports linear-versus-nonlinear probe comparisons and classification ablations testing Chain-of-Thought prompting and three-view inputs. It reports comparable average symmetry performance across probe types, minimal prompting gains, and marginal multiview gains concentrated on Johnson solids. These test additional explanations for failure, although their detailed results are deferred to the unavailable appendix.

E5.justification: V3 explicitly reports averaging symmetry accuracy across five cross-validation folds and gives a human hard-MRT standard deviation of 0.11. V1 reports single-split point estimates without these statistics. Statistical reporting expands, but fold-level variability, confidence intervals, and random-seed information remain absent from the supplied PDFs.

E6.justification: V3 reports revised cross-validated symmetry estimates and new comparator results. Its MRT results feature SigLIP at 69% and DINOv2 at 67%, replacing v1's headline ConvNeXt result of 60% under different probing and training conditions; these are not same-setting gains. New human results include 68.05% average hard-set accuracy and 90% for top performers. Geometry-native classification scores and prompting/multiview findings further expand the results.

T1.justification: Section 3.1 drops the identical-vertex-configuration requirement from the definition of a regular polyhedron, making the stated definition less restrictive. It also omits the earlier discussion of constructing duals through face centroids and polar reciprocation. The weighted cross-entropy mathematics remains unchanged; no new theorem or proof is supplied.

C1.justification: The central contribution remains GIQ as a benchmark exposing geometric-reasoning weaknesses. V3 qualifies its MRT conclusion by acknowledging that the strongest nonlinear configuration matches average human performance. Its conclusion also extends the diagnostic claim by presenting GIQ skills as necessary foundations for understanding complex scenes.

C2.justification: V3 adds substantial interpretations concerning nonlinear accessibility of representations, prompting limitations, and occlusion versus geometric reasoning. The conclusion introduces hypotheses about noisy training priors and texture-based approximations, while acknowledging that transfer to arbitrary organic shapes remains untested and future training requires broader real-world distributions. These go substantially beyond v1's largely descriptive account of failures.

D1.justification: V3 newly specifies that non-reconstruction tasks retain complex backgrounds, explicitly identifies reconstruction evaluation as zero-shot, and documents synonym handling with manual verification for classification. These disclosures do not establish changes to the earlier experiments. Conversely, Section 3.3 omits v1's environment-emitter radiance of (0.3, 0.3, 0.3). The dataset access destination is unchanged.

R1.justification: V3 adds citations for the geometry-native comparators, model providers, and historical sources, while dropping some earlier geometry and representation references. Its central positioning against generic object datasets and earlier spatial-reasoning benchmarks remains largely unchanged. Citation-style and publication-metadata updates do not constitute additional scientific repositioning.

P1.justification: The abstract and introduction are extensively rewritten; geometry and reconstruction-model descriptions are condensed; the lengthy model-by-model error discussion becomes grouped error categories; and the conclusion is substantially expanded and reorganized. The principal section sequence remains, but the editorial revision extends well beyond inserting new experimental content.

P2.justification: V1's polyhedral-group table becomes compact Figure 2, while its symmetry table and MRT plots become the paired Figure 3. Reconstruction examples shrink from six displayed rows to four. The classification/results display is redesigned as Figure 4, showing two rather than four illustrated reasoning cases. Hard-pair examples and several detailed results are redirected to an appendix absent from the supplied v3.

improvement.justification: V3 substantially strengthens benchmark validation through shape-disjoint cross-validation, nonlinear probes, geometry-native comparators, and a measured human baseline (Sections 4.2–4.4; Figures 3–4). These address important weaknesses in v1's reliance on one symmetry split, linear readouts, and assumed human superiority, while making the MRT conclusion more nuanced. The gains outweigh reduced visible detail and localized definition/presentation regressions. Missing referenced appendices and unsupported extrapolations to general spatial intelligence nevertheless limit verification and claim strength.
